messages.subject: Mediation vs. Moderation
parts:
Hi all,

I am doing a study that was testing a moderation model (with the lm function) and mediation model with two mediators (which I was conducting in lavaan). While the goal wasn't originally to compare the two models, the reviewers want us to compare AIC values so I transferred the lm model to lavaan and was able to replicate the estimates. The AIC for the mediation model was much higher (~17000 compared to ~9000). And I want to understand if that means anything and it not, explain it to the reviewer.

My understanding is that the number of parameters was higher in the mediation model because there were more intercepts and variances to estimate. Also my understanding is that in the moderation model there is one DV but in the mediation model, there would be three (the original DV plus two of the covariates in the moderation turned into mediators. Therefor, both the number of parameters and the difference in DVs would make the two AICs not only difference, but that I would not be able to compare them due to the difference DVs. Is this correct? Or would I be able to compare the models even with the different DVs. I've looked around and see some people say they've compared mediation vs moderation models and others say you can't, so I am not sure what is acccurate.

My moderation model tested the interaction between each of the two potential moderators in separate models. So, simplified, my first moderation model was:

moderation1 <-'
DV ~ IV + Mod1 + Mod2 + IVxMod1 + control1 + control2 
'
In my mediation model, the moderators were now potential mediators. so simplified was:
Mediation <- '
DV ~ IV + Med1 + Med2 + control1 + control2 
Med1 ~ IV  + control1 + control2 
Med2 ~ IV  + control1 + control2
Med1 ~~ Med2
' 
Are the AICs meaningful to compare and/or is there a way to get a meaningful comparison even with the difference parameters and DVs?

Thank you ,
Mark

messages.subject: Re: Mediation vs. Moderation
parts:
Well, even if that doesn't help you ... Moderation is something completely different from mediation. If your theoretical foundation is sound, then there is nothing to compare here. Sometimes you have to educate the reviewers. I wouldn't get involved in that game. Just my 2 cents.

Best

Christian

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Mediation vs. Moderation
parts: I am trying to understand if the changes between the models would make the loglikelihoods not comparable.

They are not.  Even if Mod1 == Med1 and Mod2 == Med2, your moderation model includes an additional variable (IVxMod1) that is not in the mediation model.  Thus, the models are fitted to different sample covariance matrices (compare lavInspect(fit, "sampstat") from the 2 models to see).  There may also be an issue with using the default fixed.x=TRUE because (if Mod1 == Med1 and Mod2 == Med2) the moderators are exogenous in the moderation model (i.e., their sample stats are taken as given, not estimated) but endogenous in the mediation model.  

If Mod1 == Med1 and Mod2 == Med2, I suppose you could make likelihoods comparable by setting fixed.x=FALSE and including IVxMod1 in the mediation model as a saturated covariate (i.e., it can covary with everything else's residuals, so it does not affect your df).  

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: 87ea943af675adaa
messages.subject: Re: Mediation vs. Moderation
parts:
Thank you!!! This is very helpful. If I understand correctly:
1. The AICs are not comparable due both to the inclusion of the interaction term in the moderator and the endogeneity of the mediators in the in the mediation model.
2. If I wish to compare AICs, I would need to enter the interaction term in the mediator model and changed fixed.x to FALSE.
3. If I do #2, I would be able to compare overall model fit, yet the parameter estimates would slightly change due to the inclusion of the interaction term (and possibly due to fixed.x = T).
4. If I want to both look at the AIC and the parameter estimates, I could first do #2 above to compare the AIC, and, if the mediation model appears to have a better fit, I could run the mediation model as I originally did without the interaction and with fixed.x = T to look at the parameter estimates.

If that all correct?
Thank you for your help.
Mark
